statement: ▶ Remark 4. Some methods for reducing the number of queries of a good LTC are also known. Specifically, by [12, Thm. 3.11, Prop. 3.6], if there exists a good q-query LTC satisfying some assumptions (which are satisfied by the good LTCs of [9]) on alphabet Σ, then there exists a good 2-query LTC with alphabet Σ′ ⊆ Σq . A different construction of this kind, which also needs assumptions on the LTC, appears in [25, Cor. 3.4]. It is further known that the existence of a good weak F-linear LTC implies the existence of a good weak 3-query F-linear LTC [6, Thm. A.1]. We do not know if there is a query complexity reduction method that works for a general good LTC.

Proof Idea Our alphabet reduction method for LTCs (Theorems 2 and 3) is simple in nature and consists of concatenating2 the given 2-query LTC C ⊆ Σn with a special code D ⊆ ∆k (which remains fixed as n grows) and showing that the concatenated code C ◦ D ⊆ ∆nk is also a good 2-query LTC. While concatenation is a well-known method for reducing a good code’s alphabet size, it usually fails to preserve the property of being a 2-query LTC. The novelty of our approach is in showing that the inner code D ⊆ ∆k (and the identification of Σ with D) can be chosen so that the property of being a 2-query LTC will persist. Let us now explain in more detail how our concatenation approach works in the context of Theorem 2(i). To begin, let us first see why C ◦ D ⊆ ∆nk is in general not a 2-query LTC. statement: The final cause for loosing on the soundness is the replacement of T by a ∆-separable tester. In more detail, in the non-linear case, the trick is to first guess what are the two letters that will be read by T , and apply T only if these letters are actually encountered (otherwise accept the word). This multiplies the soundness by a factor of |Σ|−2 . We do not know how to avoid this factor in general. However, in the linear case, T is morally close to being ∆-separable (it is always ∆m -separable for m = ⌈ 2dim dim Σ ∆ ⌉), and one can use a different trick which reduces the soundness by a factor of O(log |Σ|).

Relation to Other Works on Alphabet Reduction Concatenation with the “ordinary” long code and Hadamard code was used in the literature for alphabet reduction in the construction of PCPs and 2-query LTCs. For example, in [8, §§7–8], resp. [20, §6.4], this technique is used to construct non-linear, resp. linear, weak 2-query LTCs having linear distance and inverse-polylogarithmic rate. The same method was pushed further in [25] to construct (strong) F2 -linear 3-query LTCs (with a binary alphabet) and F2 -LTCs with an 8-letter alphabet having similar distance and rate. In a nutshell, the idea of these alphabet reductions is to encode both the letters and the constraints of the code; this is different from our approach which encodes only the letters. To explain this, let us describe an oversimplified version of the alphabet reduction of [8]: We start with a code C ⊆ Σn having a 2-query tester T . Choose some embedding of Σ in {0, 1}t and use it to view words in Σn as strings of tn bits. Think of T as checking at random one of (say) R 2-letter constraints which define C ⊆ Σn . Since Σ ⊆ {0, 1}t , every such constraint is a circuit on 2t bits. Now construct a new code C ′ ⊆ {0, 1}N by modifying the codewords w ∈ C as follows. First, view w as a tn-bit string using that Σ ⊆ {0, 1}t . Then, for each of the R constraints defining C, attach to w the long-code encoding of the 2t 2t bits participating in that constraint.3 This results in a string of N = tn + 22 R bits, and we take C ′ to be the collection of all such strings. Since the long-code encoding of 2t bits includes the evaluation of any circuit on those bits, if w′ ∈ {0, 1}N is obtained from some w ∈ Σn by the above procedure, then we can emulate the action of T on w by reading just 1 bit from w′ . The long code4 has two additional relevant properties. First, it has a 22t 3-query tester.
